screens.title: Core Ansible Modules for System Management
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll meet the core Ansible modules you will use every day to keep systems in the state you expect. These modules — package, systemd, service, user, group, file, copy, template, command, and shell — are the workhorses that make automation predictable and idempotent. You will see how ansible. builtin. package provides a single task to install or remove software across distributions, how systemd and service control running services, and how file, copy, and template let you manage content and permissions reliably. We'll also cover user and group management and the important distinction between the command and shell modules so you know when a specific module is the safer, more idempotent choice. A concrete example you will build in the hands-on is an nginx web server playbook that installs the package, ensures the service is enabled and started, and deploys a custom index. html. Common mistakes, like using shell for tasks that have dedicated modules or forgetting owner and mode on files, will be discussed and demonstrated. By the end, you'll be able to choose the correct module for routine system tasks and write playbook tasks that change state only when required.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Core Ansible Modules
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Core Ansible Modules for System Management

Automate package installs, service control, account management, and file deployment using modules designed for idempotent, cross-distribution operation. This chapter focuses on practical patterns and common pitfalls.

Why this matters
Fewer manual steps, consistent system state across hosts, and safer, auditable changes.
Concrete outcome
By following the hands-on, you will deploy nginx, start and enable its service, and place an index.html file with correct ownership and permissions.
Visual Concept
Package
ansible.builtin.package installs or removes software across distros.
Service
systemd or service modules manage runtime state and boot enablement.
Files
file, copy, and template control content, permissions, and rendered templates.
Commands
Use command for simple invocations, shell when you need piping or redirection.
In this lesson: package, service/systemd, user/group, file/copy/template, command vs shell. Coming up: hands-on nginx playbook.
Explore Key Topics
Package Management
Use ansible.builtin.package to write one task that works across apt, yum, dnf, and zypper.
Service Control
Prefer systemd for modern systems; service will fall back when appropriate.
Files & Templating
Use copy for static files and template with Jinja2 when you need host-specific content.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on practical, repeatable skills so you can automate core system tasks reliably. First, you'll learn to use ansible. builtin. package to manage software across distributions. This means writing a single task that installs, updates, or removes packages without caring whether the host uses apt, yum, dnf, or zypper. Second, you'll configure and control services with ansible. builtin. service and ansible. builtin. systemd. You will understand when to prefer systemd for modern Linux and when service is appropriate, and how to ensure a service is started and enabled on boot. Third, you'll manage accounts and groups using ansible. builtin. user and ansible. builtin. group so user creation, uid, home, shell, and group relationships are managed idempotently. Fourth, you'll perform file and directory operations with file, copy, and template — using copy for static assets and template plus Jinja2 when you need dynamic, host-specific rendering. Each objective includes a short example and a competency milestone so you can verify the task succeeded. These skills are the foundation for reproducible, secure system configuration.

screens.title: Learning Objectives (continued)
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on running ad hoc commands and the safety trade-offs between the command and shell modules. You will learn to prefer dedicated modules because they are typically idempotent and offer clearer error handling. When no module exists, use ansible. builtin. command for simple, atomic commands that do not require shell features. If you require pipes, redirects, or environment expansion, use ansible. builtin. shell but do so carefully because it executes through a shell and can introduce injection risks. The objective includes examples and a small verification pattern: run the playbook, check changed vs ok results, and examine the managed node to confirm idempotency. Finally, you'll be able to rationalize module selection in real situations, for example choosing package over a shell install command, or template over echoing variables into files, improving reliability and security across your automation work.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Learning Objectives

Distinguish command and shell

Understand when a shell is necessary and the security implications of running through a shell.

ansible.builtin.command
Runs an executable directly, without shell processing. Safer and preferred for simple commands.
Example: running a simple check that does not require pipes or redirection.
ansible.builtin.shell
Runs through a shell so you can use expansion, pipes, and redirects. Use carefully and sanitize variables.
Example: a command that needs a pipe or environment expansion.
Common mistake
Overusing shell for tasks covered by modules reduces idempotency and increases risk. Prefer dedicated modules when available.

screens.title: Ansible modules and idempotency
screens.narratorSegment: An Ansible module is a small unit of work that enacts a change or verifies a state on a managed node. Think of modules as the tools Ansible uses to reach a declared desired state. A critical property of most core modules is idempotency: running the same task repeatedly will not change the system after the desired state is reached. That means you can run playbooks frequently without causing unintended side effects. For example, a package task with state: present will only install a package if it is missing; if the package is already present, the task reports ok rather than changed. The concrete benefit is predictable automation and simpler troubleshooting because changes only happen when they are necessary. A common misconception is that playbooks must be imperative sequences; instead, declare states and let modules converge the system. As a quick check, run a task twice: the first run may show changed, the second should show ok. Why does idempotency matter for teams? It reduces risk, simplifies rollbacks, and lets you confidently apply automation repeatedly. Consider this as the foundational discipline for all subsequent module usage.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Ansible modules and idempotency
Definition

What a module does

Modules perform the actual changes on managed nodes. They are written to make tasks idempotent so running a playbook multiple times converges to the same state.

• Idempotency example: a package task with state: present only installs when the package is missing.
• Team benefit: repeatable automation reduces surprises and manual intervention.
• Misconception: using shell makes tasks easier; often it makes them less safe and less idempotent.
Key Takeaway

Express state, not steps. Trust modules to make minimal changes and keep repeated runs safe.

Quick demo snippet
- name: Ensure Nginx package is installed
  ansible.builtin.package:
    name: nginx
    state: present

# Running this task twice will install nginx once; subsequent runs report ok.
Try running the task twice. First run shows changed when it installs. Second run shows ok because idempotency prevented repeat changes.

screens.title: Package Management with ansible.builtin.package
screens.narratorSegment: The ansible. builtin. package module is the recommended, distribution-agnostic way to manage software. It acts as an abstraction layer over native package managers such as apt, yum, dnf, and zypper so a single task can work across different Linux flavors. A common usage is name: nginx with state: present to ensure a package is installed, state: latest to update it, or state: absent to remove it. The power here is simplicity and idempotency: you do not need to write conditional tasks per distribution. As a concrete example, the playbook task to ensure nginx is present is compact and readable. One misconception to avoid is trying to run a shell command like yum install nginx -y; this may work but it bypasses idempotency and error handling that the module provides. When troubleshooting, check the task results: changed indicates the module performed an action, ok means the state already matched. For multi-package operations use a list under name or the packages parameter, and test both initial installation and subsequent runs to confirm idempotency. This pattern keeps playbooks maintainable as inventories grow. Package Management with ansible.builtin.package means use ansible.builtin.package to write distribution-agnostic package tasks that remain idempotent and clear.. In practical terms, write one task that works across apt, yum, dnf, and zypper. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Package Management
Usage

ansible.builtin.package

Install, update, or remove packages in a cross-distribution way. Prefer this over raw package manager commands.

  • state: present installs if missing
  • state: latest upgrades to the latest available version
  • state: absent removes the package
Key Takeaway

Use package for simple, idempotent package tasks that run across distros.

Code example
- name: Ensure Nginx package is installed
  ansible.builtin.package:
    name: nginx
    state: present

- name: Remove an old package
  ansible.builtin.package:
    name: httpd
    state: absent
Tip: test the task twice. The first run may change the system; the second should not. If it does, review the task inputs for non-idempotent parameters.

screens.title: Service control: ansible.builtin.service vs ansible.builtin.systemd
screens.narratorSegment: Managing services is a common administrative task and Ansible provides two primary modules for it: ansible. builtin. service and ansible. builtin. systemd. The service module covers older init systems like SysVinit or Upstart and will often fall back to systemd when available, while ansible. builtin. systemd offers more direct, systemd-specific features and is the preferred choice on modern distributions where systemd is the init system. Both modules support state parameters such as started, stopped, restarted, and enablement flags like enabled: yes. As a concrete example, to ensure sshd is running and enabled on boot you can use systemd with name: sshd state: started enabled: yes. A common misconception is that service always works everywhere; while it often does, using systemd on systemd hosts gives you access to finer controls and clearer semantics. When writing playbooks, document which init system you expect or use conditional checks in inventory facts. Testing the service task on a target host and confirming the enabled state on reboot ensures your automation is reliable across environments. Service control: ansible.builtin.service vs ansible.builtin.systemd means prefer systemd on modern linux for precise control; service is useful for older systems or for compatibility.. In practical terms, choose the right module for your target init system. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Service vs Systemd
ansible.builtin.systemd

Preferred for modern systems

Use systemd for hosts that run systemd. It supports start, stop, restart, enable, and fine-grained options specific to systemd.

- name: Ensure SSH service is running and enabled (using systemd)
  ansible.builtin.systemd:
    name: sshd
    state: started
    enabled: yes
ansible.builtin.service

Compatibility with older init systems

Use service for SysVinit or Upstart, or when you prefer a module that can fall back across init systems.

- name: Restart Apache service (using service module for older systems)
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: httpd
    state: restarted
Pro tip
If your inventory mixes init systems, use a conditional that chooses systemd when ansible_facts indicate it, otherwise fall back to service for compatibility.

screens.title: User and group management with user & group modules
screens.narratorSegment: Managing users and groups declaratively keeps system identity consistent and auditable. The ansible. builtin. user module creates, modifies, or removes user accounts and lets you specify attributes such as uid, group membership, home directory, shell, and a hashed password. The ansible. builtin. group module manages groups and can ensure a particular gid exists. A typical use case is creating a deployment user with a fixed UID and group membership so services run with predictable permissions. For example the user task named deployuser sets uid, group, home, shell, and state: present. These modules are idempotent: if a user already exists with the given attributes, Ansible reports ok. A common mistake is attempting to manage passwords in plaintext or neglecting to supply a hashed password; follow your team's secret-management practice. When applying user changes, verify ownership of application directories afterwards because user and group changes can alter file ownership semantics. The takeaway is to manage identity as code and test the result by confirming the user exists with the expected properties. User and group management with user & group modules means use user and group modules to declare accounts and group membership so identity is reproducible and auditable.. In practical terms, create and maintain accounts idempotently. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › User & Group Management
ansible.builtin.user

Manage user accounts

- name: Create a new deployment user
  ansible.builtin.user:
    name: deployuser
    uid: 2001
    group: developers
    home: /home/deployuser
    shell: /bin/bash
    state: present
Confirm created user properties with inventory facts or getent on the managed node after running the playbook.
ansible.builtin.group

Manage groups

- name: Ensure 'developers' group exists
  ansible.builtin.group:
    name: developers
    gid: 5000
    state: present
Groups let you assign permissions and keep user memberships consistent across hosts. Verify gid and members when auditing systems.

screens.title: Managing files and directories with file
screens.narratorSegment: The ansible. builtin. file module is the canonical way to create or manage files, directories, and symlinks with explicit ownership and permissions. Use state: directory to ensure a directory exists with the desired owner, group, and mode. Use state: touch to ensure a file exists. Because file is idempotent, Ansible will only change permissions or ownership when they differ from the declared values. A practical example is ensuring an application log directory exists with owner myappuser, group myappgroup, and mode '0755'. A common error is forgetting to set owner or mode, which can leave services unable to write logs or access configuration. When combined with copy or template, file helps prepare the filesystem layout before deploying content. Always verify permissions after applying changes—on some systems umask or ACLs introduce nuances. Treat file tasks as part of a predictable provisioning sequence: create directories first, then copy or render files into place with correct ownership and mode. Managing files and directories with file means use file to ensure directories and permissions exist before copying or templating content into them.. In practical terms, set permissions, ownership, and directory state reliably. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › File module
Why use file

Ensure filesystem properties

  • Create directories with state: directory
  • Set owner, group, and mode declaratively
  • Make operations idempotent and predictable
Common pitfall
Not setting owner or mode can lead to permission issues for services that need to read or write files.
Example
- name: Ensure application log directory exists
  ansible.builtin.file:
    path: /var/log/myapp
    state: directory
    owner: myappuser
    group: myappgroup
    mode: '0755'
After creating directories, copy or template files into them and verify ownership to avoid runtime errors.

screens.title: Copy vs Template: static files and Jinja2 rendering
screens.narratorSegment: Copy and template are both used to place files on managed nodes, but they serve different needs. Use ansible. builtin. copy when the content is static and does not require variable rendering. Copy preserves ownership and mode and is straightforward for distributing configuration files or static H T M L. Use ansible. builtin. template when the file needs dynamic content: the template module renders a Jinja2 template on the control node using variables and writes the result to the managed node. A typical template use is inserting host-specific values like a hostname into a motd or configuration. The chapter shows templating with src: templates/nginx. conf. j2 and dest: /etc/nginx/nginx. conf. Templates are powerful but require correct Jinja2 syntax; a template error prevents the file from rendering. A common misconception is to use shell to echo variables into a file—templates give readable, maintainable results and are idempotent. When testing, render a template and check that the variables were substituted as expected on the managed host. Copy vs Template: static files and Jinja2 rendering means use copy for static content and template when you need jinja2 to inject variables into files before deployment.. In practical terms, when to copy and when to render with template (jinja2). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Copy vs Template
ansible.builtin.copy

Copy a static file from the control node to the managed node. Good for distributing images, HTML, or fixed configuration files.

- name: Copy custom index.html
  ansible.builtin.copy:
    src: files/index.html
    dest: /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
    owner: nginx
    group: nginx
    mode: '0644'
ansible.builtin.template

Render a Jinja2 template on the control node and deploy the result. Use when content needs variables like hostnames or environment values.

- name: Deploy templated Nginx configuration
  ansible.builtin.template:
    src: templates/nginx.conf.j2
    dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
    owner: root
    group: root
    mode: '0644'
Misconception
Avoid using shell to create files with variables. Templates are more maintainable and idempotent than manual echo or heredoc commands run via shell.

screens.title: ansible.builtin.command vs ansible.builtin.shell
screens.narratorSegment: Both command and shell let you run arbitrary commands on managed nodes, but they differ in capability and risk. The command module executes a program directly and does not process shell features like pipes, redirection, or shell variable expansion. This makes command safer for atomic commands because it reduces injection risk and keeps intent explicit. The shell module runs through a shell, enabling pipes, redirects, and complex expressions, which is useful when you need those features. However, shell is more powerful and therefore more dangerous if untrusted input is used. The best practice is to prefer a dedicated module for common tasks—for example, using ansible. builtin. package to install a package instead of running yum install via shell. If you must use shell, sanitize inputs and avoid constructing commands from unsanitized variables. A concrete example: instead of command: yum install nginx -y, use the package module which preserves idempotency and better error handling. Always check changed vs ok to see whether your command tasks are idempotent in practice. ansible.builtin.command vs ansible.builtin.shell means use command for simple calls that don't need shell features, and prefer modules whenever they exist.. In practical terms, understand capabilities and risks of each module. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. ansible.builtin.command

Execute a program directly without shell processing. Safer for simple tasks.

# Example: a simple command
- name: List /tmp directory
  ansible.builtin.command:
    cmd: ls -la /tmp
ansible.builtin.shell

Runs through a shell, enabling pipes, redirects, and expansions. Use carefully and sanitize inputs.

screens.title: Common mistakes and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: There are a few recurring mistakes learners make when automating system tasks with Ansible. First, over-reliance on shell or command when a dedicated module exists undermines idempotency and error handling. For example, using a shell task to install packages loses the cross-distro abstraction and makes subsequent runs harder to reason about. Second, forgetting to set owner, group, or mode for files and directories can lead to permission issues for services or users; always declare these attributes explicitly when they matter. Third, templating errors are common — Jinja2 syntax mistakes prevent a file from rendering and can break deployment. Validate templates locally and test template rendering in a dry run. A good process is: 1) choose the specific module when available, 2) declare owner/group/mode for files and directories, 3) test templates for syntax, and 4) run playbooks twice to confirm idempotency. Following this short checklist reduces surprises and makes automation robust enough for teams and CI systems. Common mistakes and best practices means prefer modules, set permissions, validate templates, and test idempotency by running tasks twice.. In practical terms, avoid shell overuse, set file ownership, and validate templates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. keyIdea.title: Nginx starter checklist
keyIdea.text: Install package, ensure service state, and deploy a static index.html with correct ownership and mode.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Hands-on Nginx
Starter Playbook
---
- name: Setup Nginx web server
  hosts: webservers
  become: yes
  tasks:
    - name: Install Nginx package
      ansible.builtin.package:
        name: nginx
        state: present

    - name: Ensure Nginx service is running and enabled
      ansible.builtin.systemd:
        name: nginx
        state: started
        enabled: yes

    - name: Copy custom index.html
      ansible.builtin.copy:
        src: files/index.html
        dest: /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
        owner: nginx
        group: nginx
        mode: '0644'
Files directory
Place index.html under files/ next to this playbook. Contents can be <h1>Hello from Ansible Nginx!</h1>.
Run and verify
Run ansible-playbook and confirm changed vs ok, then check the server in a browser.
Extend
Later swap copy for template to render host-specific content with Jinja2.

Question 1

Create /opt/appdata with 0770 ownership

Choose modules that express desired state. This makes automation repeatable and reduces manual maintenance across many hosts.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll meet the core Ansible modules you will use every day to keep systems in the state you expect. These modules — package, systemd, service, user, group, file, copy, template, command, and shell — are the workhorses that make automation predictable and idempotent. You will see how ansible. builtin. package provides a single task to install or remove software across distributions, how systemd and service control running services, and how file, copy, and template let you manage content and permissions reliably. We'll also cover user and group management and the important distinction between the command and shell modules so you know when a specific module is the safer, more idempotent choice. A concrete example you will build in the hands-on is an nginx web server playbook that installs the package, ensures the service is enabled and started, and deploys a custom index. html. Common mistakes, like using shell for tasks that have dedicated modules or forgetting owner and mode on files, will be discussed and demonstrated. By the end, you'll be able to choose the correct module for routine system tasks and write playbook tasks that change state only when required.

These objectives focus on practical, repeatable skills so you can automate core system tasks reliably. First, you'll learn to use ansible. builtin. package to manage software across distributions. This means writing a single task that installs, updates, or removes packages without caring whether the host uses apt, yum, dnf, or zypper. Second, you'll configure and control services with ansible. builtin. service and ansible. builtin. systemd. You will understand when to prefer systemd for modern Linux and when service is appropriate, and how to ensure a service is started and enabled on boot. Third, you'll manage accounts and groups using ansible. builtin. user and ansible. builtin. group so user creation, uid, home, shell, and group relationships are managed idempotently. Fourth, you'll perform file and directory operations with file, copy, and template — using copy for static assets and template plus Jinja2 when you need dynamic, host-specific rendering. Each objective includes a short example and a competency milestone so you can verify the task succeeded. These skills are the foundation for reproducible, secure system configuration.

This second objectives slide focuses on running ad hoc commands and the safety trade-offs between the command and shell modules. You will learn to prefer dedicated modules because they are typically idempotent and offer clearer error handling. When no module exists, use ansible. builtin. command for simple, atomic commands that do not require shell features. If you require pipes, redirects, or environment expansion, use ansible. builtin. shell but do so carefully because it executes through a shell and can introduce injection risks. The objective includes examples and a small verification pattern: run the playbook, check changed vs ok results, and examine the managed node to confirm idempotency. Finally, you'll be able to rationalize module selection in real situations, for example choosing package over a shell install command, or template over echoing variables into files, improving reliability and security across your automation work.

An Ansible module is a small unit of work that enacts a change or verifies a state on a managed node. Think of modules as the tools Ansible uses to reach a declared desired state. A critical property of most core modules is idempotency: running the same task repeatedly will not change the system after the desired state is reached. That means you can run playbooks frequently without causing unintended side effects. For example, a package task with state: present will only install a package if it is missing; if the package is already present, the task reports ok rather than changed. The concrete benefit is predictable automation and simpler troubleshooting because changes only happen when they are necessary. A common misconception is that playbooks must be imperative sequences; instead, declare states and let modules converge the system. As a quick check, run a task twice: the first run may show changed, the second should show ok. Why does idempotency matter for teams? It reduces risk, simplifies rollbacks, and lets you confidently apply automation repeatedly. Consider this as the foundational discipline for all subsequent module usage.

The ansible. builtin. package module is the recommended, distribution-agnostic way to manage software. It acts as an abstraction layer over native package managers such as apt, yum, dnf, and zypper so a single task can work across different Linux flavors. A common usage is name: nginx with state: present to ensure a package is installed, state: latest to update it, or state: absent to remove it. The power here is simplicity and idempotency: you do not need to write conditional tasks per distribution. As a concrete example, the playbook task to ensure nginx is present is compact and readable. One misconception to avoid is trying to run a shell command like yum install nginx -y; this may work but it bypasses idempotency and error handling that the module provides. When troubleshooting, check the task results: changed indicates the module performed an action, ok means the state already matched. For multi-package operations use a list under name or the packages parameter, and test both initial installation and subsequent runs to confirm idempotency. This pattern keeps playbooks maintainable as inventories grow. Package Management with ansible.builtin.package means use ansible.builtin.package to write distribution-agnostic package tasks that remain idempotent and clear.. In practical terms, write one task that works across apt, yum, dnf, and zypper. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Managing services is a common administrative task and Ansible provides two primary modules for it: ansible. builtin. service and ansible. builtin. systemd. The service module covers older init systems like SysVinit or Upstart and will often fall back to systemd when available, while ansible. builtin. systemd offers more direct, systemd-specific features and is the preferred choice on modern distributions where systemd is the init system. Both modules support state parameters such as started, stopped, restarted, and enablement flags like enabled: yes. As a concrete example, to ensure sshd is running and enabled on boot you can use systemd with name: sshd state: started enabled: yes. A common misconception is that service always works everywhere; while it often does, using systemd on systemd hosts gives you access to finer controls and clearer semantics. When writing playbooks, document which init system you expect or use conditional checks in inventory facts. Testing the service task on a target host and confirming the enabled state on reboot ensures your automation is reliable across environments. Service control: ansible.builtin.service vs ansible.builtin.systemd means prefer systemd on modern linux for precise control; service is useful for older systems or for compatibility.. In practical terms, choose the right module for your target init system. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Managing users and groups declaratively keeps system identity consistent and auditable. The ansible. builtin. user module creates, modifies, or removes user accounts and lets you specify attributes such as uid, group membership, home directory, shell, and a hashed password. The ansible. builtin. group module manages groups and can ensure a particular gid exists. A typical use case is creating a deployment user with a fixed UID and group membership so services run with predictable permissions. For example the user task named deployuser sets uid, group, home, shell, and state: present. These modules are idempotent: if a user already exists with the given attributes, Ansible reports ok. A common mistake is attempting to manage passwords in plaintext or neglecting to supply a hashed password; follow your team's secret-management practice. When applying user changes, verify ownership of application directories afterwards because user and group changes can alter file ownership semantics. The takeaway is to manage identity as code and test the result by confirming the user exists with the expected properties. User and group management with user & group modules means use user and group modules to declare accounts and group membership so identity is reproducible and auditable.. In practical terms, create and maintain accounts idempotently. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The ansible. builtin. file module is the canonical way to create or manage files, directories, and symlinks with explicit ownership and permissions. Use state: directory to ensure a directory exists with the desired owner, group, and mode. Use state: touch to ensure a file exists. Both command and shell let you run arbitrary commands on managed nodes, but they differ in capability and risk. The command module executes a program directly and does not process shell features like pipes, redirection, or shell variable expansion. This makes command safer for atomic commands because it reduces injection risk and keeps intent explicit. The shell module runs through a shell, enabling pipes, redirects, and complex expressions, which is useful when you need those features. However, shell is more powerful and therefore more dangerous if untrusted input is used. The best practice is to prefer a dedicated module for common tasks—for example, using ansible. builtin. package to install a package instead of running yum install via shell. If you must use shell, sanitize inputs and avoid constructing commands from unsanitized variables.
